source_text: Ναί, φασίν· ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ σάρξ, ὥστε καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀναγκάζειν συναμαρτάνειν αὐτῇ, μάτην κατηγοροῦντες αὐτῆς καὶ τὰ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων ἁμαρτήματα μόνῃ περιτιθέντες. Ποῦ γὰρ καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἁμαρτῆσαι ἡ σὰρξ δυνήσεται, ἐὰν μὴ τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχῃ προηγουμένην καὶ προκαλουμένην αὐτήν; Ὥσπερ γὰρ ζεῦγος βοῶν λυθέντων ἀπ' ἀλλήλων τοῦ ζυγοῦ τῶν βοῶν οὐδέτερος αὐτῶν κατ' ἰδίαν ἀροῦν δύναται, οὕτως οὐδὲ ψυχὴ καὶ σῶμα λυθέντα τῆς συζυγίας καθ' ἑαυτὰ ποιῆσαί τι δύνανται. Eἰ δὲ καὶ ἡ σὰρξ μόνη ἁμαρτωλός, μόνης ταύτης ἕνεκεν ἦλθεν ὁ σωτήρ, καθώς φησιν· Oὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν. Ἐπειδὴ οὖν τιμία παρὰ θεῷ καὶ ἔνδοξος παρὰ πάντα τὰ ποιήματα δέδεικται ἡ σάρξ, δικαίως ἂν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ σωθήσεται. Λεκτέον οὖν πρὸς τοὺς λέγοντας ὅτι, εἰ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα τοῦ θεοῦ ποίημα τυγχάνει οὖσα καὶ τιμία αὐτῷ παρὰ πάντα, οὐκ εὐθέως καὶ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἔχει. Καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον τὸ μετὰ τηλικαύτης βουλῆς γενόμενον καὶ παρὰ πάντα τὰ λοιπὰ τίμιον περιορᾶν τὸν ποιήσαντα εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι; Eἶτα ὁ μὲν πλάστης καὶ ζωγράφος, εἰ τὰς εἰκόνας, ἃς ἂν ποιήσωσι, διαμένειν ἐθέλουσιν, ἵνα δι' αὐτῶν δοξάζωνται, φθειρομένας αὐτὰς ἀνακαινοποιοῦσιν· ὁ δὲ θεὸς τὸ αὐτοῦ κτῆμα καὶ πλάσμα περιεῖδεν ἂν ὡς τὸ μὴ ὄν, μηκέτι δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ εἶναι; Ματαιοπόνον ἀποκαλοῦμεν, ὥσπερ εἴ τις οἰκίαν οἰκοδομήσας ἔπειτα καταλύοι, ἢ καταλελυμένην περιορῴη, δυνάμενος ἀναστῆσαι· τὸν δὲ θεὸν οὐκ αἰτιασόμεθα, ὅτι μάτην ποιεῖ; Ἀλλ' οὐχ ὁ ἄφθαρτος τοιοῦτος, οὐκ ἄφρων ὁ τῶν ὅλων πέφυκε νοῦς. Eὐφημείτωσαν οἱ ἄπιστοι, εἰ τὸ μὴ πιστεύειν ἔχουσιν αὐτοί! Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ κέκληκεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν καὶ ἐπαγγέλλεται τὴν αἰωνίαν ζωήν. Ἔνθα γὰρ τὸν ἄνθρωπον εὐαγγελίζεται σῶσαι, καὶ τῇ σαρκὶ εὐαγγελίζεται. Τί γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλ' ἢ τὸ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος συνεστὸς ζῶον λογικόν; Μὴ οὖν καθ' ἑαυτὴν ψυχὴ ἄνθρωπος; Oὔκ· ἀλλ' ἀνθρώπου ψυχή. Μὴ οὖν καλοῖτο σῶμα ἄνθρωπος; Oὔκ· ἀλλ' ἀνθρώπου σῶμα καλεῖται. Eἴπερ οὖν κατ' ἰδίαν μὲν τούτων οὐδέτερον ἄνθρωπός ἐστι, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἀμφοτέρων συμπλοκῆς καλεῖται ἄνθρωπος, κέκληκε δὲ ὁ θεὸς εἰς ζωὴν καὶ ἀνάστασιν τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οὐ τὸ μέρος ἀλλὰ τὸ ὅλον κέκληκεν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ τὸ σῶμα. Ἐπεὶ πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον, ἀμφοτέρων ὄντων κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ, τὸ μὲν σώζειν, τὸ δὲ μή; Oὐκ ὄντος γὰρ ἀδυνάτου, καθάπερ δέδεικται, τὴν σάρκα ἔχειν τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν, τίς ἡ διάκρισις, ὥστε τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν σώζεσθαι, τὴν δὲ σάρκα μή; Ἢ φθονερὸν ποιοῦσι τὸν θεόν; Ἀλλὰ ἀγαθός ἐστι καὶ σώζεσθαι πάντας θέλει· καὶ δὴ αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ κηρύγματος αὐτοῦ οὐχὶ μόνον ἤκουσεν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν καὶ σὺν αὐτῇ ἡ σάρξ, καὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἀλλ' ἀμφότερα ἐλούσαντο καὶ ἀμφότερα τὴν δικαιοσύνην εἰργάσαντο. Ἀρ' οὖν ἀχάριστον ἢ ἄδικον ἀποφαίνουσι τὸν θεόν, εἰ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων πιστευόντων ἐπ' αὐτὸν τὴν μὲν σώζειν θέλει, τὴν δὲ οὔ; Ναί, φασίν· ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν ψυχή ἐστιν ἄφθαρτος, μέρος οὖσα τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐμφύσημα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἴδιον καὶ συγγενὲς ἠθέλησεν σῶσαι· ἡ δὲ σὰρξ φθαρτὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ καθάπερ ἡ ψυχή. Eἶτα τίς αὐτῷ χάρις; Καὶ τίς ἐπίδειξις τῆς δυνάμεως καὶ χρηστότητος αὐτοῦ, εἰ τὸ μὲν φύσει σωζόμενον καὶ μέρος ὑπάρχον αὐτοῦ σώζειν ἤμελλεν; Aὐτὸ γὰρ ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ εἶχε τὴν σωτηρίαν, ὥστε τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν σώζων οὐ μέγα ποιεῖ· τὸ γὰρ σώζεσθαι πάρεστιν αὐτῇ, ὅτι ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ μέρος, ἐμφύσημα αὐτοῦ οὖσα. Ἀλλ' οὐδὲ χάρις αὐτῷ τὸ ἴδιον σώζοντι· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ἑαυτὸν σώζειν. Ὁ γὰρ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ σώζων δι' ἑαυτοῦ ἑαυτὸν σώζει, μή ποτε ἐκεῖνο τὸ μέρος ἐνδεὲς γένηται. Oὐκ ἔστιν ἀγαθοῦ τὸ τοιοῦτον. Oὐδὲ γὰρ ἄνθρωπον ἀγαθόν τις ἐρεῖ τὸν τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐγγόνοις χαριζόμενόν τι. Τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ τὰ ἀγριώτατα τῶν θηρίων ποιοῦσι· κἂν ὑπεραποθανεῖν τῶν ἐκγόνων αὐτῶν δέῃ, ἑκοντὶ τοῦτο ὑπομένουσιν. Eἰ δέ τις τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς δούλοις παράσχοι, δικαίως ἂν οὗτος λέγοιτο ἀγαθός. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς ἀγαπᾶν τοὺς ἐχθρούς, ἐπεὶ τίς ὑμῖν χάρις; φησίν. Ὥστε δέδειχεν ἡμῖν ἀγαθὸν ἔργον εἶναι τὸ μὴ τοὺς ἐξ αὐτοῦ γεγονότας μόνον ἀγαπᾶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἔξωθεν. Ἂ δὲ ἡμῖν παρήγγειλε πολὺ πρότερον αὐτὸς ἐποίει. ***
pass_a_gloss: Yes, they say; but the flesh is sinful, so that it also forces the soul to sin with it, vainly accusing it and attributing the sins of both to it alone. For where could the flesh sin by itself, if it did not have the soul leading and calling it? Just as when a yoke of oxen is loosed from each other, neither of them can plow alone, so also the soul and body, having been loosed from their yoking, cannot do anything by themselves. But if the flesh alone is sinful, the Savior came for its sake, as he says: I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Since, then, the flesh has been shown to be precious and glorious to God, beyond all his creations, it will rightly be saved by him. We should say to those who claim that, even if the flesh is the best of God's creations and precious to him, it does not immediately have the promise of resurrection. And how is it not absurd that, after such great counsel and being precious beyond all else, the Creator would abandon it to no longer exist? The craftsman and painter, if they want their creations to remain so that they may be glorified through them, restore them when they are decaying; will God, then, abandon his own possession and creation as if it were nothing, no longer existing? We call this idle work, just as if someone were to build a house and then tear it down, or were to overlook a ruined house when they could restore it; we will not accuse God of doing something in vain. But the incorruptible and all-encompassing mind is not like this. Let the unbelievers praise such a thing, if they have unbelief! But, in fact, he has also called the flesh to resurrection and promises it eternal life. For where he preaches the gospel to save humanity, he also preaches it to the flesh. For what is a human, if not a rational living being composed of soul and body? Is the soul, then, a human by itself? No, but the soul of a human. Is the body, then, called a human? No, but the body of a human. If, then, neither of these is a human by itself, but the combination of both is called a human, and God has called humanity to life and resurrection, he has called not the part but the whole, which is the soul and the body. How is it not absurd, when both exist together and in the same thing, to save one and not the other? For since it has been shown that the flesh can have rebirth, what is the distinction, so that the soul is saved but the flesh is not? Or do they make God envious? But God is good and wants all to be saved; and, in fact, both our soul and our flesh have heard his gospel and believed in Christ Jesus, and both have been washed and both have worked righteousness. Do they, then, show God to be ungrateful or unjust, if he wants to save one of the two that have believed in him, but not the other? Yes, they say; but the soul is incorruptible, being a part of God and his breath, and for this reason he wanted to save his own and kindred thing; the flesh, however, is corruptible and not from him, as the soul is. What, then, is his gratitude? And what is the display of his power and goodness, if he was going to save what is naturally saved and is a part of him? For it had salvation from him, since it is his part, his breath; saving the soul is not a great thing, for it is present to it because it is his part. But there is no gratitude in saving his own thing; this is the same as saving himself. For the one who saves his part through himself saves himself, lest that part ever be in need. This is not characteristic of what is good. For no one would call a person good who shows favor to their children and descendants; even the wildest of beasts do this, and they would even endure death for their offspring. But if someone were to show the same favor to their slaves, they would rightly be called good. For this reason, the Savior also taught us to love our enemies, since what gratitude is there in that? He says. So he showed us that it is a good work not to love only those who come from him, but also those outside. And what he commanded us to do, he did himself long before.

choices.why: The verb ἀναγκάζειν means to compel or force someone to do something.
The noun συζυγία refers to the act of yoking or joining two things together.
The noun ἐπαγγελία refers to a promise or pledge.
The noun ἀνάστασις refers to the act of rising or standing up, often used to describe the resurrection of the dead.
The noun πλάσμα refers to something that is created or formed.

bible_refs.note: I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

pass_b_english: Yes, they say the flesh is sinful, and so it forces the soul to sin along with it; they accuse the flesh in vain, heaping the sins of both onto it alone. For how could the flesh sin by itself if it did not have the soul leading and urging it on? It is like a yoke of oxen unloosed from each other: neither can plow alone. In the same way, once soul and body are loosed from their union, neither can do anything by itself. But if the flesh alone is sinful, then the Savior came for its sake, just as he said: "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Matthew 9:13). Since the flesh has been shown to be precious and glorious to God beyond all his works, it will rightly be saved by him. We must answer those who claim that, even if the flesh is the noblest of God's works and precious to him, it does not therefore possess the promise of resurrection. How is it not absurd that, after such great deliberation and being honored above all else, the Creator would abandon it to non-existence? A craftsman or painter who wants their works to endure so they may be glorified through them will restore them when they decay; would God then abandon his own possession and creation as if it were nothing, letting it cease to be? We call that futile labor, like someone who builds a house only to tear it down, or ignores a ruined house when able to rebuild it; we would not accuse a human of doing such a thing in vain, so how much less God? But the incorruptible, all-encompassing Mind is not like this. Let the unbelievers praise such a notion, if that is what their unbelief leads them to! In fact, he has called the flesh to resurrection and promises it eternal life. For where he proclaims the gospel to save the human being, he proclaims it to the flesh as well. What is a human being, if not a rational living creature composed of soul and body? Is the soul by itself a human being? No, it is the soul of a human being. Is the body by itself called a human being? No, it is called the body of a human being. Since neither is a human being on its own, but the human being is the combination of both, and since God has called the human being to life and resurrection, he has called not a part but the whole, which is soul and body together. When both exist together in the same reality, how is it not absurd to save one and not the other? Since it has been demonstrated that the flesh can experience rebirth, what distinction justifies saving the soul but not the flesh? Are they making God out to be envious? But God is good and desires all to be saved. Indeed, both our soul and our flesh have heard his gospel and believed in Christ Jesus; both have been washed, and both have worked righteousness. Do they therefore portray God as ungrateful or unjust, if he wills to save one of two believers but not the other? They answer: yes, but the soul is incorruptible, being a part of God and his breath, and so he wished to save what is his own and akin to him; the flesh, however, is corruptible and not from him as the soul is. What grace is there in that? And what display of his power and goodness, if he only saves what is naturally saved and is already a part of him? The soul possessed salvation from him by its very nature, since it is his part, his breath; saving the soul is no great thing, for salvation is inherent to it precisely because it is his part. But there is no grace in saving what is one's own; that is simply saving oneself. The one who saves his own part through himself saves himself, lest that part ever be in need. That is not the mark of the good. No one calls a person good merely for showing favor to their children and descendants; even the wildest beasts do that, and they would even die for their offspring. But if someone shows the same favor to their slaves, they would rightly be called good. For this reason the Savior also taught us to love our enemies, since he asked: "What credit is that to you?" He showed us that a good work consists not in loving only those who come from us, but also those outside. And what he commanded us to do, he himself did long before.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. Scripture citations (Matthew 9:13) are correctly identified and added to the translation as required. The distinction between the soul as 'breath' (ἐμφύσημα) and its relation to God is preserved.
